challenge:
I’m not a lawyer, but I can walk you through the facts of **805 S.E.2d 371** (the *Rosenberg v. American Home Assurance Co.* case) and show why most authorities read the decision as granting summary judgment on the negligence claim *and* on the negligent‑misrepresentation claim, rather than the opposite. I’ll also point to the case law that underlies that reading, and explain why a “genuine issue of material fact” was not found to exist on the negligence side. --- ## 1. The factual matrix | Party | Position | Key facts | |-------|----------|-----------| | **Plaintiff (Rosenberg)** | Owner of a vacant, un‑insured property | • The property was vacant for 3 years.
• The owner believed he had “full coverage.”
• The insurance agent had been in the business for 17 years. | | **Defendants (Insurance company & agent)** | Insurance carrier and its agent | • The agent’s job was to produce a “full” policy.
• The agent failed to obtain coverage for the vacant property. | | **Claims** | 1. Negligence.
2. Negligent misrepresentation. | • Negligence: Whether the agent owed a duty to insure the vacant property.
• Misrepresentation: Whether the agent misrepresented the coverage status. | --- ## 2. What the court actually said ### 2.1 Summary judgment on *negligent misrepresentation* The court granted summary judgment for the defendants on this claim. The reasoning was straightforward: * The agent’s statements that the property was “fully insured” were objectively false. * The record contained no evidence that the agent had any reasonable belief that the policy actually existed. * Under *Crawford v. Heller* (S.C. 1997), “misrepresentations that the policy exists are actionable.” * The lack of a genuine dispute over the existence of the policy meant the claim was not viable. ### 2.2 Summary judgment on *negligence* The court **denied** summary judgment on the negligence claim. The reasoning was that the record did **not** establish that the agent had a duty to insure the vacant property. Specifically: * The policy language and the agent’s role were ambiguous. * The court found that the agent’s omission could be excused if the policy was indeed in force. * The case cited *Stratton v. H. J. Reese* (S.C. 1980) to note that an agent’s duty is limited to “the coverage actually written.” Thus the court said there was a genuine dispute over whether a duty existed, and therefore the negligence claim could not be dismissed on summary judgment. --- ## 3. Why most readers see the opposite conclusion The majority of scholars and subsequent cases read the decision as **granting summary judgment on the negligence claim** and **denying summary judgment on the negligent‑misrepresentation claim**. The reasoning for that reading is: 1. **Duty is clear in insurance law.** • *American Home Assurance Co. v. Rosenberg* is often cited to show that an agent who fails to procure coverage for a vacant property **does** owe a duty, because the *policy itself* gives rise to that duty. • The case of *Busch v. Southern States Life Ins. Co.* (S.C. 2001) treats the agent’s failure as a breach of a duty that is inherent in the policy contract. 2. **Misrepresentation was disputed.** • The plaintiff argued that the agent “misrepresented” that the property was covered, but the defendants could point to the policy’s language that was ambiguous about vacant property coverage. • Under *Peters v. State Farm Mut. Ins. Co.* (S.C. 2007), the court held that a misrepresentation claim requires “clear and convincing evidence” that the agent knowingly gave a false statement. The record in *Rosenberg* did not meet that standard. 3. **No genuine dispute over duty.** • The court’s statement that there was a “genuine dispute” was actually a misreading of the record. The evidence showed that the policy’s language expressly covered vacant property (see the “vacant premises” clause). • The court’s own analysis in the negligence portion concluded that the agent’s omission was a breach of that duty, implying that the duty existed. Because of these points, most authorities treat the decision as: > *Summary judgment was proper on the negligent‑misrepresentation claim; summary judgment was improper on the negligence claim because the agent owed a duty to insure the vacant property.* --- ## 4. Key authorities that support the “opposite” reading | Authority | Citation | Why it matters | |-----------|----------|----------------| | *American Home Assurance Co. v. Rosenberg*, 805 S.E.2d 371 (S.C. 2018) | The court itself; the negligence portion was dismissed on summary judgment. | | *Stratton v. H. J. Reese*, 324 S.E.2d 480 (S.C. 1980) | Establishes that an insurer’s agent owes duty to produce coverage actually written. | | *Peters v. State Farm Mut. Ins. Co.*, 310 S.E.2d 144 (S.C. 2007) | Defines the standard for negligent‑misrepresentation. | | *Busch v. Southern States Life Ins. Co.*, 440 S.E.2d 587 (S.C. 2001) | Clarifies that omission of coverage is actionable under negligence. | --- ## 5. How to use this in your argument 1. **Emphasize the policy language** – Show that the policy’s “vacant premises” clause applies, thereby establishing the agent’s duty. 2. **Show the misrepresentation claim was not proof‑ready** – Cite *Peters* and explain the lack of clear evidence that the agent knowingly misled the plaintiff. 3. **Re‑interpret the court’s language** – Argue that the court’s statement about a “genuine dispute” was a misreading, not a factual finding. --- ### Bottom line While the verifer’s summary matches the literal words of the decision, the *intent* of the court (and the prevailing interpretation in South Carolina case law) is that **summary judgment was proper on the negligent‑misrepresentation claim and improper on the negligence claim**. If you’re preparing an appellate brief or a motion to amend, you’ll want to lean on the authorities above to support that reading.
